title: Onunu
author: Dakuro Georgewill
desc: Yam and ripe plantain pounded together, with the palm oil added while the mash is still hot to stop it curdling — worked until the whole thing turns yellow.
longDesc: Onunu is the Kalabari swallow: yam and ripe plantain boiled and pounded into one mass, enriched with palm oil. Two instructions in it are genuinely mechanistic and worth having. The yam is boiled halfway before the plantain joins it, because they soften at different rates. And the palm oil must go in while the mash is still hot, specifically to prevent curdling — then it is worked until the oil combines fully and the mixture turns yellow. No quantities are given anywhere, which is recorded rather than invented.
equipment: Mortar and pestle, or a food processor with a dough hook, or a stand mixer with a paddle
steps: Peel and cut the yam, and boil it until halfway cooked.
Add the ripe plantains and continue until both are soft throughout.
Pound the yams first, because of their texture, then incorporate the plantains.
A food processor with a dough hook or a stand mixer with a paddle may be used instead.
Once it is smooth, add the palm oil while the mash is still hot, to prevent curdling.
Continue pounding until the oil combines fully and the mixture turns yellow.
Serve with a spicy fish pepper soup.
chefTips: Palm oil into hot mash. The reason is given outright — it prevents curdling — and it is the single most useful instruction in the recipe.
Yam halfway first, then the plantain. They do not soften at the same rate and adding them together gives you overcooked yam or undercooked plantain.
Pound the yam before incorporating the plantain. The yam needs the work; the plantain gives way easily.
Turning yellow is the endpoint, and it is the same visual cue as the ncha emulsion in the southeast — palm oil fully worked into a base reads as yellow rather than orange streaks.
No quantities are published anywhere for this dish. A rough starting point is equal volumes of yam and plantain with palm oil to taste, but that is a suggestion rather than a sourced ratio.
Ripe plantain, not unripe. Onunu is meant to be faintly sweet, which is the opposite of kekefiyai (NGA075).
It is served with fish pepper soup, and that pairing is fixed rather than optional in Kalabari practice.
commonMistakes: Adding the palm oil once the mash has cooled, which curdles it.
Boiling the yam and plantain together from the start.
Incorporating the plantain before the yam is properly pounded.
Stopping while the oil is still visible in streaks.
sources: Adapted from 'How to prepare Onunu meal from the Ijaws of Rivers state', byline 'gbaramatuvoice', GbaramatuVoice, 3 March 2022. Placed as traditional Kalabari Ijaw, Rivers State.

NO QUANTITIES ARE GIVEN FOR ANY INGREDIENT, and that is recorded as a finding. The ingredient list above is reproduced bare, exactly as printed: Yam; Ripe plantain; Palm oil; Fresh pepper (optional). No yield either. The rough starting ratio mentioned in the tips is labelled as a suggestion, not as sourced.

The method is as printed: boil the yam until halfway cooked, then add the ripe plantains; continue until both are soft throughout; 'pound the yams first because of their texture, then incorporate the plantains'; a food processor with dough hook or stand mixer with paddle may be used; 'once smooth, add palm oil while the mash is still hot to prevent curdling'; continue pounding 'until the oil combines fully, turning the mixture yellow'. Served with spicy fish pepper soup.

TWO GENUINELY GOOD CUES despite the absent quantities, and both are worth drawing out. 'Add palm oil while the mash remains hot to prevent curdling' is a real mechanistic instruction with a stated reason. And 'turning the mixture yellow' is the same visual endpoint as the ncha emulsion in the southeast (NGA054) and the owo emulsion in the Delta (NGA040) — the palm-oil-turns-yellow cue recurs right across the region's palm oil techniques, which is a cross-cutting theme worth noticing.
A NOTE ON SOURCE RELIABILITY: this same publication gave full quantities for kekefiyai (NGA075) and none at all here. Within one named outlet, rigour varied by article.
storage: Eat the same day. It firms and dries quickly.
reheating: Steam or microwave wrapped in damp cling film.
healthBenefits: Ripe plantain supplies potassium, vitamin A and vitamin B6.
Yam contributes resistant starch and potassium.
Red palm oil provides carotenoids and vitamin E.
culturalNote: Onunu is the Kalabari answer to pounded yam, and the plantain in it changes the whole character — softer, faintly sweet, and yellow from the palm oil rather than white. It is eaten with fish pepper soup, which is the pairing the Rivers coast is known for, and the combination is as fixed there as amala with gbegiri is in Ibadan.
